items.title: What the strategy may see
items.prose: A backtest engine loops over the bars one at a time. It has just reached the close of bar 4 and is about to call `decide(history)`. Orders go out for the next open.
items.question: Tap every row that `history` may contain.

feedback.correct: `history` holds bars 1 to 4, the bars that have finished.
feedback.generic: The engine stands at the close of bar 4. Which bars have finished by then?

byKey.all: You gave the strategy the whole table. The engine hands over only what exists at that moment.
byKey.next: Bar 5 opens after this close. The order fills there, but the decision cannot see it.
byKey.r0: An older bar is still history. The strategy may read it.
byKey.r1: An older bar is still history. The strategy may read it.
byKey.r2: An older bar is still history. The strategy may read it.
byKey.r3: Bar 4 has just closed, so its close is known. It belongs in `history`.
byKey.r4: Bar 5 has not started. Its prices do not exist at the close of bar 4.
byKey.r5: Bar 6 is two bars in the future.

explain.text: The engine stands at the close of bar 4, so bars 1 to 4 exist and nothing later does. The order it creates waits for the open of bar 5. A strategy that reads bar 5 is looking into the future.

items.title: Who is in the universe on 15 June 2021
items.prose:
A share is in the universe on a date if it passes three tests:

- it is listed on the date
- it has a full 60 days of history
- its 60-day mean volume is at least £5m

We may use only what was known on 15 June 2021. A dash means no figure exists.
items.question: Tap every share in the universe on 15 June 2021.

feedback.correct: AAA, EEE and FFF pass all three tests on that date.
feedback.generic: Test each share on 15 June 2021: listed then, a full 60-day window, and volume of at least £5m.

byKey.survivors: You dropped EEE because it dies in November. On 15 June it is listed and liquid, so it belongs.
byKey.r0: AAA is listed, old enough and liquid. Keep it.
byKey.r1: BBB's last day was 3 March 2021. It is gone by 15 June.
byKey.r3: DDD lists in August. A universe built on 15 June cannot know it.
byKey.r4: EEE dies in November, but on 15 June it is listed and liquid. A point-in-time universe keeps it.
byKey.r5: £5.0m meets 'at least £5m'. The rule is inclusive.
byKey.r6: GGG listed on 4 May, about 30 trading days ago. It has no full 60-day window yet.

explain.text: AAA, EEE and FFF pass. BBB has died, DDD has not listed, CCC is too thin, and GGG lacks a 60-day window. A point-in-time universe keeps EEE, which dies later.

items.title: Quotes the cleaner removes
items.prose:
One-month calls on a £100 share. The cleaner keeps a quote only if all four hold:

- the bid is above 0
- the bid is not above the ask
- the age is at most 30 minutes
- (ask − bid) / mid is under 0.5
items.question: Tap every quote the cleaner removes.

feedback.correct: Four quotes fail a rule: stale, zero bid, crossed and too wide.
feedback.generic: Check each row against the four rules in turn. A quote that fails any one is removed.

byKey.r0: The £90 quote is 95 minutes old, past the 30-minute limit.
byKey.r1: The £95 quote is fresh, and its spread of 0.30 on a mid of 5.95 is only 5%. It stays.
byKey.r2: The £100 quote passes all four rules. It stays.
byKey.r3: A zero bid fails the first rule, however small the ask.
byKey.r4: The bid of 0.30 is above the ask of 0.20, so the quote is crossed.
byKey.r5: The spread of 0.08 equals the mid of 0.08, a ratio of 1.0. That is too wide.
byKey.r6: Spread 0.04 on a mid of 0.12 is 33%, under 0.5. Cheap is not wide.

explain.text: £90 is stale, £105 has no bid, and £110 is crossed. £115 has a spread as big as its mid. £120 is cheap, but its spread is a third of the mid, so it stays.

items.title: The cost of one fill
items.prose: The engine buys 3,000 shares at £42.50. Commission is £0.005 a share with a £1 minimum. The half spread is 2 basis points of the traded value.
items.question: What does the fill cost in total, in £?

feedback.correct: Commission £15.00 plus half spread £25.50 is £40.50.
feedback.generic: Add two costs. Commission is shares times £0.005, and the half spread is 2 bp of shares times price.

byKey.spread-only: You charged the spread but not the commission. The engine charges both.
byKey.commission-only: You charged the commission but not the half spread. Crossing the spread costs real money.
byKey.full-spread: You charged the whole spread, 4 bp. A fill pays half of it, 2 bp.

explain.text: Commission is 3,000 × £0.005 = £15.00, above the £1 minimum. The traded value is 3,000 × £42.50 = £127,500, and 2 bp of it is £25.50. The total is £40.50.

items.title: Twelve-minus-one on monthly returns
items.prose: Monthly log returns of one share, in percent, to the end of December. The 12-minus-1 signal is the sum of the first 11 months, skipping the latest month.
items.question: What is the 12-minus-1 signal, in percent?

feedback.correct: January to November sum to 15%.
feedback.generic: Add the monthly returns from January to November. December is the month we skip.

byKey.all-twelve: You added December's −5 as well. The skip month is left out on purpose.
byKey.latest-only: −5 is December alone, the month that reverses. The signal is the other eleven.
byKey.dropped-oldest: You dropped January and kept December. The skip removes the latest month, not the oldest.

explain.text: The first eleven months sum to 15. December's −5 is skipped, because one-month returns tend to reverse.

items.title: One Newton step
items.prose: We solve for the implied volatility of a one-year at-the-money call by Newton's method. The share is £100, the strike £100, $r = 5\%$, no dividend. The market mid is £13.00. At $\sigma = 25\%$ the model price is £12.34 and vega is 37.8, the price change per 1.00 of volatility.
items.question: Take one Newton step from 25%. What is the new volatility, in percent?

feedback.correct: The model is £0.66 too cheap, so volatility must rise by 0.66 / 37.8, about 1.75 points.
feedback.generic: Newton's step is $\sigma_1 = \sigma_0 + (\text{market} - \text{model}) / \text{vega}$. Keep volatility in decimals while you divide.

byKey.minus: You moved volatility down. The model price is below the market, so volatility has to go up.
byKey.no-vega: You added the price gap straight to volatility. Divide by vega first.
byKey.units: You added a decimal step of 0.0175 to 25 points. Convert before you add.

explain.text: The gap is 13.00 − 12.34 = 0.66. Divided by vega 37.8 it is 0.0175, so the new volatility is 0.25 + 0.0175 = 0.2675, or 26.75%. The true implied volatility is 26.75%, so one step is already close.

items.title: One bar of the engine loop
items.prose: Orders fill at the next open. The engine keeps one order waiting from the previous bar. Here are the steps it takes on each new bar.
items.question: Put the steps of one bar in the order the engine runs them.

lines.text: Fill the order left over from yesterday, at today's open
Mark equity: cash plus shares at today's close
Give the strategy the history up to today's close
Turn the strategy's signal into a target position
Turn the change in target into an order for tomorrow's open

feedback.correct: Fill at the open, then the close of the bar can be used, then the decision, then the order.
feedback.generic: Work out what each step needs. The fill needs yesterday's order. The new order needs the target, and the target needs the signal.

byKey.s1: Yesterday's order fills first, at the open. Nothing from today's close is known yet.
byKey.s2: Equity is marked at the close, after the fill has changed cash and shares.
byKey.s3: The strategy sees today's close only after the bar has ended, so after the open fill.
byKey.s4: The target comes from the signal, so the signal step must run first.
byKey.s5: The order is the last step. It needs the target, which needs the signal.

explain.text: The old order fills at today's open, before anything about today's close exists. Marking equity and handing over the history both wait for the close. Signal, target and order follow, and the order waits for tomorrow's open.

items.title: A split and a dividend on one day
items.prose: A share closes Monday at £240.00. On Tuesday it splits two-for-one and pays £1.50 per new share. Tuesday's raw close is £123.00.
items.question: What is Tuesday's total return, in percent?

feedback.correct: One old share is now two new shares, each worth £123.00 plus £1.50 in cash.
feedback.generic: Value what one Monday share has become on Tuesday: two new shares, with the dividend, against £240.00.

byKey.raw: You compared raw closes. The split halved the price, but the holder owns twice as many shares.
byKey.no-dividend: You adjusted for the split but left out the dividend. The holder also received £1.50 on each new share.
byKey.dividend-old: You paid the dividend once per old share. It is paid on each of the two new shares.

explain.text: One old share becomes two new ones, worth 2 × (123.00 + 1.50) = £249.00. Against £240.00 that is a gain of 9 / 240 = 3.75%.

items.title: The dividend yield in an option pair
items.prose: From a one-year chain, the at-the-money pair at strike £100: call mid £9.30, put mid £6.70. The share is £100 and the rate is 5% a year, continuously compounded.
items.question: What dividend yield $q$ do the two quotes imply, in percent?

feedback.correct: Parity gives a forward of £102.73, and $q = r - \ln(F/S)/T = 2.30\%$.
feedback.generic: Parity gives the forward: $F = K + e^{rT}(C - P)$. Then $F = S e^{(r-q)T}$ gives $q$.

byKey.no-discount: You added C − P to the strike without the factor $e^{rT}$. The gap is paid at expiry, so it grows at the rate.
byKey.no-rate: You solved $F = S e^{-qT}$ and left out $r$. The forward grows at $r - q$.
byKey.linear: You used $F/S - 1$ in place of $\ln(F/S)$. That is close, but the answer is off in the third figure.

items.title: Doubling the order
items.prose: Impact per £ traded is $c\,\sigma\sqrt{Q/V}$, with $c = 1$, $\sigma = 1.5\%$ a day and daily volume $V = 1{,}600{,}000$ shares. Buying 40,000 shares at £60 costs £5,692.10 in impact. We now buy 80,000 shares at the same price.
items.question: What does the 80,000-share order cost in impact, in £?

feedback.correct: The impact rate rises by $\sqrt 2$ and the traded value doubles, so the cost rises by $2\sqrt 2$.
feedback.generic: Two things change. The impact per £ grows with the square root of size, and the value traded grows with size.

byKey.linear: You doubled the cost. Impact per £ also rises when the order does, so the cost grows faster than size.
byKey.old-notional: You raised the impact rate by $\sqrt 2$ but charged it on the old £2.4m. The order is now £4.8m.

explain.text: At 80,000 shares the rate is 0.015 × √0.05 = 0.335%, up from 0.237%. It applies to £4,800,000, so the cost is £16,099.69. That is 2.83 times the smaller order.

items.title: Is the mean IC different from zero
items.prose: A signal's monthly rank IC has mean 0.036 and standard deviation 0.081 over 36 months. The months do not overlap.
items.question: What is the t statistic of the mean IC?

feedback.correct: The mean is 2.67 standard errors from zero.
feedback.generic: The standard error of a mean is the sd over $\sqrt n$. Divide the mean by it.

byKey.ir: You divided the mean by the sd. That is the information ratio of one month. The t statistic needs $\sqrt{36}$ as well.
byKey.annual-ir: You scaled the ratio by $\sqrt{12}$, as for an annual Sharpe. A t statistic scales by $\sqrt{36}$, the months you have.

explain.text: The standard error is 0.081 / √36 = 0.0135. The t statistic is 0.036 / 0.0135 = 2.67, a little above the usual 2.

items.title: Three pricers on one grid
items.prose:
Six-month puts on a £100 share, $r = 5\%$, $q = 1\%$, $\sigma = 20\%$. EU and US are 500-step European and American trees. MC is 100,000 antithetic paths, with standard error se. A pricer error is one of three things:

- a European tree more than £0.01 from Black-Scholes
- a Monte Carlo price more than 3 standard errors away
- an American tree below the European one
items.question: Tap every cell that signals a pricer error.

feedback.correct: Three cells break a rule: European tree at 110, Monte Carlo at 90, American tree at 100.
feedback.generic: Test each column against its rule. Remember that an American put is allowed to be worth more than a European one.

byKey.premium: You flagged the large American premiums at 110 and 120. Early exercise adds value to deep in-the-money puts, so they are expected.
byKey.r3c2: The European tree at 110 is £0.12 from Black-Scholes, and the limit is £0.01.
byKey.r1c3: At 90 the Monte Carlo price is about 3.5 standard errors below Black-Scholes. The limit is 3.
byKey.r2c5: At 100 the American tree is £0.10 below the European tree. An American option is never worth less.
byKey.r3c3: That Monte Carlo price is 1.9 standard errors from Black-Scholes. Inside 3 is noise.
byKey.r3c5: Early exercise adds value to a put this far in the money. A premium over the European tree is expected.
byKey.r4c5: A premium of £1.52 over the European tree is expected for a put that far in the money.

explain.text: Three cells break a rule: European tree at 110, Monte Carlo at 90, American tree at 100. The large American premiums at 110 and 120 are early exercise, not error.

items.title: Lines that peek
items.prose: A colleague's engine decides at each close and fills at the next open. These lines build its inputs from daily data, where `close` is a pandas Series and `ret` its daily returns.
items.question: Which lines use information from the future? Select all that apply.

options.text: `z = (ret - ret.mean()) / ret.std()`, over the whole sample, used as the signal

options.why: Forward filling carries the last known price forward. It uses only the past.
The five-day return looks backwards, and `shift(1)` delays it by a bar. Nothing here uses a later bar.

feedback.correct: `shift(-1)`, whole-sample statistics and backfilling all bring tomorrow's data into today.
feedback.generic: Ask of each line: could it be computed at that bar's close, with nothing later in the file?

byKey.ffill: You flagged forward filling. It copies yesterday's price into a gap, so it looks only back.
byKey.lag: You flagged the shifted return. It looks back five bars and then waits a bar more.

explain.text: `shift(-1)` reads tomorrow's average. The whole-sample mean and sd include later returns, and `bfill` copies a later price into a gap. `ffill` and a lagged past return use only what was known.

items.title: A rank IC by hand
items.prose: Seven shares at the end of a month. S7 has no signal today, so it stays out. The rank IC is the correlation between the ranks of the signal and the ranks of next month's return.
items.question: What is the rank IC? Give a decimal.

feedback.correct: The sum of squared rank gaps is 14, so the IC is 0.6.
feedback.generic: Rank the six signals and the six returns, find each gap, and use $1 - 6\sum d^2 / (n(n^2 - 1))$ with $n = 6$.

byKey.pearson: You correlated the raw values. The 6.0% return pulls that up. A rank IC uses ranks only.
byKey.seven: You counted S7 in $n$. It has no signal, so it is not ranked and $n$ is 6.

explain.text: Signal ranks are 5, 2, 6, 3, 1, 4 and return ranks are 2, 3, 6, 5, 1, 4. The gaps are 3, −1, 0, −2, 0, 0, so $\sum d^2 = 14$. Then $1 - 6 \times 14 / (6 \times 35) = 0.6$.

items.title: Forward vols along a term structure
items.prose: Total variance is $w = \sigma^2 T$. The forward volatility between two expiries $T_1 < T_2$ is the volatility that carries $w_1$ to $w_2$: $\sqrt{(w_2 - w_1)/(T_2 - T_1)}$. If $w_2$ is below $w_1$ there is a calendar arbitrage, and no forward vol exists.

feedback.correct: Each pair uses total variance, a fall gives None, and bad inputs raise ValueError.
feedback.generic: Work in total variance $\sigma^2 T$, never in volatilities. Test the fall before taking a square root.

explain.text: Total variance adds up over time, so the forward variance is the difference divided by the time between. If it is negative, no volatility can fill the gap, and the pair is flagged with None. Averaging the two vols would ignore the expiries.

items.title: Reading a drawdown and a Calmar ratio
items.prose: Month-end equity of a strategy, in £k, over a year: `100 104 109 103 98 101 107 112 108 115 119 121 118.4`. Measure drawdown on these points.
items.question: Fill in the three measures.

rows: Maximum drawdown (%, as a positive number)

feedback.correct: The worst fall is 109 to 98, and growth is 18.4%, so Calmar is about 1.82.
feedback.generic: Track the running peak. Drawdown is the value over the peak so far, minus 1, at its worst point.

byKey.global-range: Measure each fall from the peak so far, not from the highest to the lowest point overall.
byKey.r2c1: Calmar is the yearly growth over the size of the maximum drawdown.
byKey.global-calmar: You divided by the highest-to-lowest range, not the largest fall from a running peak.

explain.text: The peak of 109 is followed by a trough of 98, a fall of 11 over 109, or 10.09%. The £118.4k ends 18.4% above £100k, so Calmar is 18.4 / 10.09 = 1.82. Using 121 and 98 would give 19.0% by comparing a trough with a later peak.

items.title: Rank weights for a long-short book
items.prose: Eight shares, one signal each. Build dollar-neutral rank weights: centre the ranks on their mean, then scale so the absolute weights sum to 1. S6 has no signal today.
items.question: Fill in the missing weights, as decimals.

feedback.correct: Seven ranked shares give centred ranks from −3 to 3, divided by 12.
feedback.generic: Rank only the seven shares with a signal. Centred ranks run from −3 to 3 and sum in absolute value to 12.

byKey.r5c2: S6 has no signal, so it is not ranked. Its weight is zero, and the other seven are ranked among themselves.
byKey.r3c2: S4 sits in the middle of the seven, so its centred rank is 0 and so is its weight.
byKey.r0c2: S1 ranks sixth of seven, a centred rank of 2. Divide by 12.
byKey.r2c2: S3 ranks first of seven, a centred rank of 3. Divide by 12.
byKey.r7c2: S8 ranks second from the bottom, a centred rank of −2. Divide by 12.

explain.text: Ranked from the bottom, the shares run S5, S8, S2, S4, S7, S1, S3, with mean rank 4. Centred ranks are −3 to 3, which sum to 12 in absolute value. S3 gets 3/12 = 0.25.

items.title: Explaining a day's P&L
items.prose: One call: delta 0.5977, gamma 0.0274, vega 0.2736 per volatility point, theta −0.0222 a day. Over one day the share rises £3, volatility rises 2 points and a day passes. Full repricing shows the call up £2.4155.
items.question: Fill in the Greek terms, their total and the residual, in £.

feedback.correct: The Greeks explain £2.4414 of the £2.4155 move. The residual is −£0.0259.
feedback.generic: Delta times the move. Half gamma times the move squared. Vega per point times the points. Theta times the days.

byKey.no-half: The gamma term is $\tfrac12 \Gamma\,dS^2$. You may have left out the half.
byKey.vega-scale: Vega here is per volatility point, so multiply by 2 points, not by 0.02.
byKey.r5c1: The residual is the actual change minus the explained total.

explain.text: Delta gives 0.5977 × 3 = 1.7931 and gamma 0.5 × 0.0274 × 9 = 0.1233. Vega gives 0.2736 × 2 = 0.5472 and theta −0.0222. The total is 2.4414, and the residual against 2.4155 is −0.0259.

items.title: One line of a tear sheet
items.prose:
A backtest gives daily equity and the weight held each day, as a fraction of equity. The conventions are the course's.

- Sharpe: $\sqrt{\text{periods}}$ times the mean over the sample sd (ddof 1) of simple returns. It is 0.0 for fewer than two returns or no spread.
- Maximum drawdown: the worst fall from a running peak, a fraction of at most 0.
- CAGR: $(E_{\text{last}} / E_{\text{first}})^{\text{periods}/(n-1)} - 1$ for $n$ values.
- Calmar: CAGR over the size of the maximum drawdown, or `math.inf` with no drawdown.
- Turnover: the mean absolute daily change in weight over all $n$ days, with weight 0 before day 1.
items.question: Write `tear_line(equity, weights, periods=252)` returning `(sharpe, max_drawdown, calmar, turnover)`.

widget.starter:
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

def tear_line(equity, weights, periods=252):
    """(sharpe, max_drawdown, calmar, turnover) of one backtest."""
    r = equity.pct_change().dropna()
    # sqrt(periods) * mean / sample sd; 0.0 if undefined
    sharpe = ...
    # worst fall from a running peak, a fraction <= 0
    max_dd = ...
    # growth per year from the first to the last value
    cagr = ...
    # cagr / |max_dd|; inf when there is no drawdown
    calmar = ...
    # mean |change in weight| per day, starting from 0
    turnover = ...
    return sharpe, max_dd, calmar, turnover
widget.solution:
import math
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

def tear_line(equity, weights, periods=252):
    """(sharpe, max_drawdown, calmar, turnover) of one backtest."""
    eq = pd.Series(equity, dtype=float)
    r = eq.pct_change().dropna()
    sd = r.std(ddof=1) if len(r) > 1 else 0.0
    sharpe = 0.0 if not sd > 1e-12 else float(np.sqrt(periods) * r.mean() / sd)
    max_dd = float((eq / eq.cummax() - 1).min())
    cagr = float((eq.iloc[-1] / eq.iloc[0]) ** (periods / (len(eq) - 1)) - 1)
    calmar = cagr / abs(max_dd) if max_dd < 0 else math.inf
    w = np.asarray(weights, dtype=float)
    turnover = float(np.abs(np.diff(w, prepend=0.0)).mean())
    return sharpe, max_dd, calmar, turnover

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

feedback.correct: All four numbers follow the course's conventions, including the edge cases.
feedback.generic: Check each convention in turn. The Sharpe uses ddof 1. The drawdown uses a running peak. The CAGR exponent is periods over n − 1.

explain.text: Each number has one convention that is easy to miss. The Sharpe uses the sample sd, the drawdown a running peak, and the CAGR n − 1 returns. A curve that never falls has no drawdown, so its Calmar is infinite.

items.title: What costs leave of a book
items.prose: A long-short book earns 5.4% a year gross, with volatility 3.0%. Over a year it trades 4.5 times its value, buys and sells together. Each £1 traded costs 14 bp in spread and impact.
items.question: Fill in the four quantities.

rows: Cost over the year (% of the book)

feedback.correct: Costs take 0.63% and net Sharpe falls from 1.80 to 1.59. Costs of 120 bp would remove all the return.
feedback.generic: Cost is traded value times cost per £. The break-even cost is the gross return divided by the value traded.

byKey.r0c1: Multiply 4.5 by 14 bp. That is a share of the book, so 63 bp or 0.63%.
byKey.r2c1: Divide the net return, not the gross, by the volatility.
byKey.r3c1: At break-even the cost equals the gross return. Divide 5.4% by 4.5.

explain.text: The cost is 4.5 × 14 bp = 63 bp, or 0.63%. Net return is 5.4 − 0.63 = 4.77%, and net Sharpe is 4.77 / 3.0 = 1.59. Costs of 5.4% / 4.5 = 120 bp per £ would leave nothing.

items.title: A net Sharpe above 3
items.prose: A colleague runs a three-day mean-reversion rule on one share and sends this output. They want to put the net Sharpe in the results note.

items.question: What should happen first?

options.text: Report 3.02. Costs are in, so it is the net figure.
options.why: Costs do not fix a fill at the signal bar's close. That price was not available to trade at.

widget.solution:
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

def sector_zscore(signal, sector, min_names=3):
    """z-score each share against its own sector, date by date."""
    out = pd.DataFrame(np.nan, index=signal.index, columns=signal.columns)
    for name in sector.unique():
        cols = list(sector.index[sector == name])
        block = signal[cols]
        n = block.notna().sum(axis=1)
        mu = block.mean(axis=1)
        sd = block.std(axis=1, ddof=1)
        z = block.sub(mu, axis=0).div(sd, axis=0)
        ok = (n >= min_names) & (sd > 1e-12)
        out[cols] = z.where(ok, np.nan, axis=0)
    return out

items.title: Newton on a far out-of-the-money quote
items.prose: A plain Newton solver, started at 20%, meets a one-month £130 call quoted at a mid of £0.03. The share is £100 and $r = 5\%$.
items.question: What went wrong, and what is the standard fix?

options.text: The quote is below intrinsic value, so no volatility exists for it.
options.why: A call out of the money has zero intrinsic value, and £0.03 is above that. A volatility of about 37% prices it.

options.text: Newton stopped too early. Raise the cap from 50 to 500 iterations.
options.why: The second step already leaves any sane range. More iterations cannot undo that.

options.text: Vega at 20% is about 0.0006, so the step is about 50. Keep every step inside a bracket and bisect when Newton leaves it.
The £0.03 mid is stale, so the cleaner should have removed it.
options.why: Staleness is about age. The console shows a step that is too big, which is a solver fault, not a data fault.

feedback.correct: A tiny vega makes the Newton step huge. A bracket with a bisection fallback keeps every step in range.
feedback.generic: Read the vega column. Newton divides the price gap by it.

explain.text: Far out of the money, vega at 20% is near zero. The price gap divided by vega throws the guess to 50.6, then to a nonsense value. Bracket the volatility, for example between 0.0001 and 5, and bisect whenever a step leaves it.

items.title: A bumped gamma of zero
items.prose: Gamma by a central bump is $(V(S+h) - 2V(S) + V(S-h))/h^2$. A colleague runs it on a three-month call. From the last row they report 'zero gamma'.
items.question: What is the right reading, and which bump would you use?

options.text: Gamma really is near zero this far out of the money, so keep $h = 10^{-8}$.
options.why: The closed form gives 0.046696. The zero comes from the bump, and the rows from 0.1 down to 0.0001 agree with the closed form.

options.text: Switch to a one-sided bump, which has no round-off.
options.why: A one-sided bump still subtracts two nearly equal prices. It loses digits too, and is less accurate at the same $h$.

options.text: The error always falls as $h$ shrinks, so rerun with $h = 10^{-10}$.
options.why: Truncation error does shrink, but round-off grows like $1/h^2$. The rows get worse below 0.0001.

options.text: Rounding error: at $h = 10^{-8}$ the second difference is about $5 \times 10^{-18}$, below the rounding error of the prices. Use $h$ near 0.001 to 0.01.

feedback.correct: Truncation error falls with $h^2$ and round-off grows with $1/h^2$, so a middle $h$ is best.
feedback.generic: Compare each row with the closed-form gamma, and ask why the smallest bump is the worst.

explain.text: Truncation error shrinks with h. But subtracting nearly equal prices loses digits, and dividing by h² magnifies the loss. The rows agree with 0.046696 from 0.1 to 0.0001, and the best is near 0.001.

items.title: A put with a few exercise dates
items.prose:
A Bermudan put can be exercised only on certain dates. On a CRR tree it may be exercised at step $i$ only if $i$ is in `exercise_steps`. Step 0 is today and step $n$ is expiry, where the put always pays $\max(K - S, 0)$. At an allowed step the holder takes the larger of the hold value and $K - S_{ij}$.

The starter builds the tree and the hold values. The tree uses $u = e^{\sigma\sqrt{\Delta t}}$, $d = 1/u$ and $p = (e^{(r-q)\Delta t} - d)/(u - d)$.
items.question: Write the exercise step so that `bermudan_put` returns the right price.

widget.starter:
import numpy as np

def bermudan_put(S, K, r, sigma, T, n, exercise_steps, q=0.0):
    """CRR tree price of a put that may be exercised only at the
    given steps (0 is today, n is expiry; expiry always pays)."""
    dt = T / n
    u = np.exp(sigma * np.sqrt(dt))
    d = 1 / u
    p = (np.exp((r - q) * dt) - d) / (u - d)
    disc = np.exp(-r * dt)
    j = np.arange(n + 1)
    # payoffs at step n
    V = np.maximum(K - S * u ** (2 * j - n), 0.0)
    for i in range(n - 1, -1, -1):
        # hold value at step i
        V = disc * (p * V[1:] + (1 - p) * V[:-1])
        # exercise here only if i is an allowed step
        ...
    return float(V[0])
widget.solution:
import numpy as np

def bermudan_put(S, K, r, sigma, T, n, exercise_steps, q=0.0):
    """CRR tree price of a put that may be exercised only at the
    given steps (0 is today, n is expiry; expiry always pays)."""
    dt = T / n
    u = np.exp(sigma * np.sqrt(dt))
    d = 1 / u
    p = (np.exp((r - q) * dt) - d) / (u - d)
    disc = np.exp(-r * dt)
    allowed = set(int(s) for s in exercise_steps)
    j = np.arange(n + 1)
    V = np.maximum(K - S * u ** (2 * j - n), 0.0)      # payoffs at step n
    for i in range(n - 1, -1, -1):
        V = disc * (p * V[1:] + (1 - p) * V[:-1])      # hold value at step i
        if i in allowed:
            nodes = S * u ** (2 * np.arange(i + 1) - i)
            V = np.maximum(V, K - nodes)               # exercise value
    return float(V[0])

explain.text: The backward loop already gives the hold value at each step. At an allowed step we replace it by the larger of hold and exercise, node by node. With no allowed step the price is European, and with every step allowed it is American.

widget.solution:
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

def net_book(signal, ret, half_spread_bp, every=5, min_names=4):
    """Daily gross and net returns of a rank-weighted long-short book."""
    n = len(signal)
    k = signal.shape[1]
    weights = np.zeros((n, k))                # the book held over each row
    cost = np.zeros(n)                        # cost charged on each row
    w_prev = np.zeros(k)
    reb = list(range(every - 1, n, every))
    for j, p in enumerate(reb):
        s = signal.iloc[p]
        valid = s.notna().to_numpy()
        w = np.zeros(k)
        if valid.sum() >= min_names:
            r = s.rank().to_numpy()
            d = np.where(valid, r - np.nanmean(r), 0.0)
            gross = np.abs(d).sum()
            if gross > 0:
                w = d / gross
        stop = reb[j + 1] if j + 1 < len(reb) else n - 1
        weights[p + 1:stop + 1] = w
        if p + 1 < n:
            cost[p + 1] = half_spread_bp / 1e4 * np.abs(w - w_prev).sum()
        w_prev = w
    r = np.nan_to_num(ret.to_numpy(float))
    gross = (weights * r).sum(axis=1)
    out = pd.DataFrame({"gross": gross, "net": gross - cost}, index=signal.index)
    return out.iloc[reb[0] + 1:] if reb else out.iloc[0:0]

items.title: Reviewing a results note
items.prompt:
A colleague sends a results note for a five-day momentum rule on one share. It uses five years of daily bars. Its claims:

- Net Sharpe 2.4 after 2 bp a trade.
- 60 lookback and threshold settings were tried, and the best is reported. The 60 Sharpes had mean 0.5 and sd 0.7.
- Orders fill at the close of the signal bar.
- The held-out year was opened twice while tuning. Its Sharpe was 0.3, so it was averaged with the research period.
- What failed: nothing.

Write your review.

(a) Name the problems in the order you would check them, and say why that order.

(b) For two of them, give a number or a test that shows how large the problem is.

(c) Rewrite the "What failed" section so that it is honest.
items.model:
**(a) Problems, in order.**

1. *A Sharpe of 2.4 on a simple rule is a bug until proved otherwise.* I check it first. Every other number depends on the engine. I run the look-ahead test. I cut the bars at several rows and replace everything after each cut with noise. No earlier row may change.
2. *The fill.* Orders fill at the close of the signal bar, a price the rule has just seen. That is the same-bar rule, and it manufactures edge. The fix is a fill at the next open, with costs and slippage that grow with size.
3. *Selection.* The note reports the best of 60 settings. With no skill at all, the best of 60 is expected near $0.5 + 0.7 \times 2.32 = 2.12$. The reported 2.4 is only 0.4 standard deviations above that, so chance can give it.
4. *The held-out year.* It was opened twice, so it is no longer held out. Averaging it with the research period mixes a spent number into a clean one. A year of daily data has a Sharpe standard error near 1.0. So 0.3 neither confirms nor rejects the rule. Report it alone, as a single look.
5. *Costs.* 2 bp ignores commission and the impact of size. I would ask for turnover and a full cost bill.

**(b) Numbers.** A daily rule with equal-sized wins and losses needs about 57.5% winning days to reach 2.4. That solves $\sqrt{252}\,(2p-1)/\sqrt{1-(2p-1)^2} = 2.4$ for $p = 0.575$. Real daily bars rarely allow that, which supports the bug reading. For selection, the expected best of 60 no-skill settings is about 2.12, against the reported 2.4. I would also ask for the count and spread of all 60 results.

**(c) What failed.**

"The first version filled at the close of the signal bar and reached a Sharpe of 2.4. We need a look-ahead test and next-open fills before quoting any figure. We tried 60 settings, with Sharpes of mean 0.5 and sd 0.7. The best of them is close to what chance alone produces. The held-out year was opened twice during tuning, so it is no longer clean. Its Sharpe of 0.3 has a standard error near 1.0 and supports no conclusion. We do not claim an edge."

rubric.text: Treats a Sharpe of 2.4 on a simple rule as a bug first. Proposes the look-ahead test: cut, add noise after the cut, compare earlier rows.
Spots the fill at the signal bar's close as a same-bar fill. Moves it to the next open with realistic costs.
Spots the selection problem: the best of 60 is near what chance gives, about 2.1. Asks for the count and spread, or a deflated comparison.
Says the twice-opened held-out year is spent. Rejects averaging it in. Notes its Sharpe of 0.3 has a standard error near 1.
Sizes a problem with a number or test: the 57.5% hit rate, the expected maximum, or the standard error.
Writes a specific "What failed" paragraph: the bug, the 60 settings, the held-out year. Not "nothing".

explain.text: Check the engine before the statistics, then the selection, then the held-out data. A note that reports only what worked has not said what failed.
